findings.issue_text: OAuth `state` in OAuthLoginView.dispatch (src/sentry/integrations/github/integration.py:402-413) is the deterministic `pipeline.signature` rather than a per-session nonce, so it is identical for every user/session (proven by the same hardcoded state `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3` asserted across tests for different orgs and users); an attacker can learn the state from their own install flow and send a victim admin a link to `/extensions/github/setup/?code=<attacker's code>&state=<known value>` while the victim has an in-progress pipeline, causing the victim's pipeline to exchange the attacker's code, bind `github_authenticated_user` to the attacker, pass the new sender check (attacker == attacker), and link the attacker's GitHub App installation to the victim's org. Fix: bind a random per-pipeline nonce (e.g., `secrets.token_hex(16)`) into pipeline state on first dispatch and validate against that instead.

In GitHubInstallation.dispatch (~line 495), the `except Integration.DoesNotExist: return pipeline.next_step()` path proceeds to completion with no verification that the OAuth-authenticated user installed the app; the entire protection depends on the `installation.created` webhook having already created the Integration row, so with delayed/failed webhook delivery (or self-hosted instances without a reachable webhook endpoint, where integrations are only created by the pipeline), an attacker-supplied installation_id is linked to the victim's org with no sender validation at all.

`integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` (~line 502) raises an unguarded KeyError (HTTP 500) for any Integration whose metadata lacks `sender` — e.g., rows created by the pipeline itself (`get_installation_info`/`build_integration` metadata does not include `sender`, which happens whenever the installation webhook didn't create the row first) or legacy rows; use `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and treat a missing sender as a graceful failure.

Test gap in tests/sentry/integrations/github/test_integration.py:~390-400 (`test_installation_not_found`): the test submits `state=ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05`, which does not match the pipeline signature used by every other test in the file (`9cae5e…`), so it only exercises the invalid-state branch of `OAuthLoginView` and short-circuits before any installation lookup; the original scenario — GitHub API returning not-found for the installation ('The GitHub installation could not be found.') — now has zero coverage and the test name is misleading.

In OAuthLoginView.dispatch (~lines 424 and 436), `safe_urlopen(...)` (token exchange) and `get_user_info(...)` are called outside any exception handling, so network failures or non-200 responses raise and produce an unhandled 500 in the user-facing install popup; only the body read/parse is wrapped in try/except — wrap the upstream calls too and route failures to the `error()` page.

The strict sender-equality check (~lines 500-505) breaks a legitimate handoff flow: a GitHub org owner who installs the app can no longer have a different Sentry admin complete the setup (the admin OAuths as themselves → mismatch → error), and the error text ('We recommend restarting the installation process') is misleading because restarting cannot fix it — the same GitHub account must both install the app and finish the Sentry flow; this needs explicit product/error-message handling rather than the generic invalid-request page.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds OAuthLoginView to authenticate a GitHub user and later (in GitHubInstallation.dispatch) compares `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user")` against `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`, but that check only runs in the branch where an ACTIVE `Integration` row already exists. In the `except Integration.DoesNotExist: return pipeline.next_step()` branch (when `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` is missing), the code proceeds with no sender/user verification at all, despite having OAuth user info available. This makes authenticity enforcement conditional on the Integration row already existing (e.g., via webhook), leaving an unverified path for installations that aren’t yet in the DB.

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, `test_installation_not_found` no longer asserts the prior behavior (`b"The GitHub installation could not be found."`) and instead makes a second request with `state=ddd023...` (different from the state used elsewhere, e.g. `9cae5e...` asserted in `assert_setup_flow`). In `OAuthLoginView.dispatch`, a state mismatch immediately returns `error(...)` before any installation lookup logic in `GitHubInstallation`, so this test now primarily exercises the invalid-state path and no longer covers the original “installation not found” scenario suggested by its name.

adjudication_records.issue_text: In OAuthLoginView.dispatch (~lines 424 and 436), `safe_urlopen(...)` (token exchange) and `get_user_info(...)` are called outside any exception handling, so network failures or non-200 responses raise and produce an unhandled 500 in the user-facing install popup; only the body read/parse is wrapped in try/except — wrap the upstream calls too and route failures to the `error()` page.

adjudication.rationale: In `OAuthLoginView.dispatch`, the token exchange request `req = safe_urlopen(...)` and the subsequent `authenticated_user_info = get_user_info(...)` are executed outside any `try/except`. Only `safe_urlread(req).decode(...)`/`parse_qsl` is guarded. If `safe_urlopen` raises (network/timeout/DNS) or `get_user_info` raises (failed request to `/user`, non-200, etc.), the exception would bubble up and return a 500 instead of rendering the intended `error(...)` page for the install popup. This is directly visible in the diff: no exception handling surrounds those calls.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The strict sender-equality check (~lines 500-505) breaks a legitimate handoff flow: a GitHub org owner who installs the app can no longer have a different Sentry admin complete the setup (the admin OAuths as themselves → mismatch → error), and the error text ('We recommend restarting the installation process') is misleading because restarting cannot fix it — the same GitHub account must both install the app and finish the Sentry flow; this needs explicit product/error-message handling rather than the generic invalid-request page.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new OAuth step (OAuthLoginView) that binds `github_authenticated_user` from `/user` and then enforces `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user") != integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` as an error condition in `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`. This does strictly require the GitHub account that OAuths during the Sentry setup flow to match the GitHub `sender` who installed the app (as recorded in `integration.metadata`). That will block a handoff scenario where one GitHub user installs and a different GitHub user completes setup. Whether that is a “bug” vs intended security/product behavior is not verifiable from the diff alone, but the finding is diff-grounded and highlights a concrete UX/product implication: the generic `ERR_INTEGRATION_INVALID_INSTALLATION_REQUEST`/“restart the installation process” message is used for this mismatch and could be misleading if the only resolution is to use the installer’s GitHub account.
